utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Take a seat, please. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman, and good morning to you and your team. Anything before we bring in the witness? All right. Usher, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Ackerman and I would like to have a chat, if that's the word, at the end of the session, about the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the end of this session? At the end when the witness is finished. I think it's better that we finish him off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't forget, it's his birthday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are proceeding with your testimony, and hopefully we'll finish today, if you keep your answers to a minimum. And before you do so, please could you repeat your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sadikovic, and happy birthday.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, I just have a few more questions left. When we broke yesterday, you were explaining to the Court how you had been to Vecici to try and prevail on the resisters in Vecici to leave. Were you successful?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, and it still haunts me, I set off between Donji Vrbanjci and Vecici. I came across a group of people and their discussion ensued, and one of those men made me angry and I turned back. However, to this day, I am sorry that I did not truly try. Perhaps I wouldn't have managed to persuade their command, but I would have found two or three prominent villagers and talked with them. However, my conscience is clear. But somehow I feel that I could have prevailed on those people to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But did you and others in your group leave together with wives and children -- leave Kotor Varos in the convoy at the end of October?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Together with my combatants, their families, my family, I left Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you could leave, did you have to do anything in respect of the property which you and the other members of the convoy owned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: There was a form which the citizens signed before departing from Kotor Varos. I cannot remember its text exactly, but roughly that they were leaving their property to Republika Srpska, something to that effect. I can't remember the text on the form verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we may have a form, which I can show you. And while I'm looking, I'd like to ask you about one final document, please. I want you to have a look at a document which is effectively a criminal report dated the 27th of October, 1993. I don't know whether, Your Honour -- it's been -- yes, it's been handed up, I gather. Could the witness be shown a copy. Now, I know you looked at this the day before yesterday. Before being shown a copy, had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a criminal report filed against a number of people, and I think if we go to number 27, you'll see your name there.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You are -- you and the others -- and I'll come back to the others in a moment. Go to, after number 29 on the list, you'll see that the criminal report was filed, because there are reasonable grounds to suspect that during the armed clashes in Kotor Varos municipality between the 24th of July and the 2nd of November, as members of Muslim military formations, they took the lives of civilians. Now, obviously, what you've told us, you left at the end of October. As far as you are aware, did you ever take the lives of civilians in any of the time that you were in Ravne, operating in Ravne?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I claim under full responsibility that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The other people who are named, do you know all of them or some of them, between 1 and 26?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any of them in your group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly in my vicinity, no, they were not. But all of them -- no, I don't know. Somebody perhaps in Vecici, or perhaps some other place, but none of those men were in my vicinity, nor were members of the staff or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you ever made aware that you were charged, at the time that you had been charged with this offence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was through the media. Well, I wasn't listening to that, but there were some relations, some neighbours, who said they had heard on the radio that I was a war criminal, which absolutely makes no sense, and I'm quite ready to account before any court, whenever there is an independent court which observes international law, I'm quite ready to account for everything I've done, and I stand by everything I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look, in connection with documents you had to sign to leave, at Exhibit 22 -- P2243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, this document that -- are you going to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you very much. P2329. I think it's one of those which has been copied both sides, so I'll hand mine up so that Your Honours can see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is not you. This is somebody else. But it's a document that says they wish to move away and leave behind their land in Kotor and destroyed house, declare I will not join any armed formations, will not fight against the army in the interests of the Serbian Republic. The statement is done in three identical copies, of which one will be sent to the Crisis Staff, one to the population resettlement agency, and one to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Was it a document like that that you had to sign? Can you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Sadikovic. That's all I ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Sadikovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as I explained to you yesterday, you're now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Mr. Ackerman, I leave him to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I also want to wish you a happy birthday, and you must be thrilled at being able to spend your birthday here with us. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's how things turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to start my questioning with you, and let me first just sort of preliminarily suggest this to you. I am planning on completing my cross-examination of you today so that you can be finished and go home, but that will depend upon whether you listen to my questions and answer just the question I ask you. If you decide to answer more than the question, then it's likely that we will not get finished today. So please try to do that. Please just listen to the question and answer the question I'm asking you. Do you think you can do that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And please understand that I do want to be fair with you, and if there is something that you feel you absolutely have to explain to the Judges, then I'll certainly give you the opportunity to do that. So just let me know if you want to explain something, and there will be no problem with that. Because I do want to be fair with you. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. By all means, I'll do what I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I appreciate that. I want to begin with a document that I received yesterday morning, which is -- it's called proofing notes, and it's a record made by, I think, an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor as a result of conversations that were had with you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I said -- just correct it. It was done by a young intern lawyer who was sitting in, not an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was made by someone who was present during what they call a proofing session, where a discussion was had with you on 24 June. That would have been Tuesday, in preparation for your testimony here. The note that I was handed says this. It says: "Mr. Sadikovic states that he has a clear memory of the events of 11 years ago." Is that correct? Did you say that at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did say that, and I do, by and large, remember all the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And the second thing I want to ask you about from those proofing notes is this: The notes say that you explained that the changes required to the three statements that you've given to various investigators since 1997 were a consequence of problems in translation/interpretation and were not errors of fact on your behalf. Is it true that you said that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. So at least with regard to these two things that I just brought to your attention, they were translated properly and reported properly to us and in fact you said them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to have in front of you each of the three statements that you have given, and I want you to have both the B/C/S version and the English version of each of those statements. And so in just a moment, those will be handed to you and then I'll have questions of you about them. Now, you should have in front of you three statements, both in the English and B/C/S. The first one, which I'll call statement number 1, is dated 21/30 October and 27 May 1997. Do you have that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you should also have a second one, which I call statement number 2, dated 12 October of the year 2000. Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me look a minute. What I have is 12 October 2000, at least on the front of the statement, that's what it says in English. Is that the same statement that you have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's all right. It's all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then the third statement, which I call statement number 3, is dated 10 March 2001. Do you also have that one?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This third one is in English. It's fine. I've got the third one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have them in both languages, both English and B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you'll recall, on those -- on each of those three occasions when you gave statements to the investigators from the ICTY, you, of course, answered the questions in your own language; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And your answers were then translated and recorded in some way, and finally a statement was produced in English; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when that statement was completed, it was then read back to you in your own language; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you were asked to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after you had made this first statement, then the last date on it being 27 May 1997, what I call statement number 1, how did it happen that you made the second statement, that you were interviewed a second time, on 12 October of 2000? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after I read the previous statement that I had given, I saw that it did not agree. It does not change the substance of events or something. For instance, Bakir Dizdar, does it matter that I saw him on that particular day, or two or three days later? I think it was an interpretation error, but it does not really change the substance. So everything remains the same, and the only question is whether I saw him that day or two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We just talked about trying to listen to my question and answer my question. My only question is this: How did it happen that you gave a second statement? Did you ask the Prosecutors to come talk to you again or did they contact you and say they wanted to talk to you again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, just to make your question a little bit more clear, or clearer: What you're being asked is this,

utterances.speaker: MR. SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: You made a first statement, which was taken on three separate occasions, on the 21st of October, 1996; on the 30th of October, 1996; on the 27th of May of 1997. That's your first statement. What Mr. Ackerman is asking you is how come that a year later, in October of the year -- not a year later; three years later, in October of the year 2000, you make another statement to the Prosecution? Did you contact the Prosecution and tell them that you wanted to make another statement? Were you contacted by the Prosecution, or by someone else and asked for an interview again? What happened? Because usually if you make a second statement three years later, there must be a reason for it. This is what Mr. Ackerman is after. Did I make your question sound clearer, at least in layman's terms, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Better than I was doing, Your Honour. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right, Your Honours. I understand. The second took place at the invitation, in Sarajevo, that is, The Hague Tribunal has its office there, and I received an invitation to come for an interview. And as I was reading it, that is, they gave me my statement to read it, and as I was reading it, I noticed those - what shall I call them - errors, perhaps, if they are errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were told by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor that they wanted to talk to you again. Did they tell you why they wanted to talk to you again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They wanted me to clarify a number of points from my previous statement, the statement that I had given. They needed clarification, or they needed me to expand on some of the points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you get the impression that they were not totally satisfied with what you had said the first time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the impression I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you the same kind of question about the third statement. You then gave a third statement. Was that -- did you request to make that statement or did the Prosecutor's office contact you and tell you they wanted to talk to you some more?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same time as the previous time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The same situation. You were contacted and asked to give a third statement by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify this. Those were not three different statements. It's the same wording, the same text. They only asked me about certain things, a number of very specific things, from the previous text, and I provided clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the records that we have, and we just talked about it, you were interviewed and signed three separate statements. And what I'm asking you now, with this third statement of 10 March 2001, were you contacted by the Prosecutor to make an additional statement or did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honours, it was done in the same way. They invited me and I came to their office. And I provided additional clarifications upon questions being asked, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you why it was they then wanted to talk to you a third time? Did they tell you what it was that was -- that they were interested in that they hadn't asked you before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were additions to be made. Then they didn't ask me to mark the checkpoints. During my third interview, they handed me a piece of paper for me to make markings where the checkpoints had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look, first of all, at the first statement that you made. That would be the one dated -- the last date on it is 27 May 1997, and I want you to look at the English version of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you speak English or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to ask him anything about the language of the statement in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's hear what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you got that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As we talked about a moment ago with regard to the procedure used in taking these statements, what they do is create a statement in English, read that statement back to you in your language, and then ask you to sign the English version of the statement, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's how it was, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at the first page, I take it the initials there on the bottom belong to you and that you made -- you wrote your initials on there.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like you to just very briefly look at each page of this statement and confirm that you initialed each page, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. All of the pages contain my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on page 10, do you see your signature, at the bottom of page 10, under the date 27 May 1997?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see my whole signature, not merely my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what it says right above your signature, sir, is this: "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." And of course, that was read to you in your own language before you were asked to sign that statement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. But it is not the same to listen to a text being read out to you and then read through it yourself later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to look at the second statement, the one of 12 October 2000. And again, I want you to look at the English version. And first of all, I think you'll agree with me that the same procedure was used, the statement was taken in English, then read back to you in your own language, and you were asked to put your signature or initials on each page and then sign it at the end, and you did all of that, didn't you? And I want you to look at each page and confirm to us that the initials there belong to you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. All the pages bear my initials or my full signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you look at page 9, sir, the witness acknowledgment there on page 9 is actually written in your language, and I think what it says is that the statement was read to you in the Bosnian language and that it is true to the best of your knowledge and recollection. Is that what that says?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you signed that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally, I'd like you to look at the third statement, the one of 10 March 2001. And the same exercise: Look at each page and confirm that the initials are yours.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, all the pages bear my initials or signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then if you look at page 7, the witness acknowledgment now appears in both languages, and again says: "The statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." And you signed -- you signed that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, with regard to any of these statements, nobody refused to tell you what was contained in these statements; in fact, they were read to you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor made it clear to you that what they wanted from you was to tell them the truth, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they certainly gave you an opportunity to make any changes in those statements that you wished to make if you thought something in those statements was not true, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this first statement, the one from 1997, was a statement you made just about five years, and even four years, four to five years after the events that you were reporting. You were making that statement in 1996/1997; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And yesterday, and again today, I believe, when you -- shortly after you came in the courtroom, the Judge asked you to stand up and read a statement which said: "I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that statement is similar to the statement contained in these statements that you were telling the truth to the best of your ability when you gave those statements. It's a similar kind of acknowledgment, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think it was less important for you to tell the truth when you gave your statements than it was when you took that oath here yesterday and today, or more important, or the same?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you the following: For me, it's equally important, in all of these cases. Whenever I speak to anyone, not merely here before the Court, but to anyone, I always tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I was asking. Now, I'm going to go through some things that you said in these statements, sir, and this will be somewhat lengthy. It will take some time to get through it. And one of the difficulties that I will have, of course, is always finding the B/C/S version of the English. But I think we can probably work through that and find it, with your help, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin, perhaps, could furnish me with a copy of the B/C/S version of the three statements, if you have them. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand what you're getting ready to do is kind of help us with that process, and I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first subject-matter, sir, that I want to discuss with you revolves around that time when TO weapons were retrieved from Kotor Varos by the JNA. And you recall that incident, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours, I do recall that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the English version, your description of that begins at the bottom of page 5, the language: "In early April of 1992," you say, "I recall an incident where the weapons in the Kotor Varos police station were retrieved by the JNA." And you said at that time that you were working the night shift; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said in this first statement that about 2.00 a.m., a CSB inspector by the name of Savo Todorovic appeared, and you said: "He wanted me to take him on patrol and conduct a control visit within the municipality." You told us in the statement that you felt uneasy, so you took your weapon with extra rounds with you. True? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You went to -- you say you went to Maslovare and Siprage and were gone three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then this: When you returned to the police station, after you had parted from Savo Todorovic, the duty officer there at the time was a gentleman named Anto Kljajic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that Anto Kljajic said to you: Boss, they took all the weapons to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He told you that JNA soldiers in camouflage uniforms had appeared with three or four trucks and removed -- and this is what you said he told you: And removed all the TO weapons which were stored in the SUP basement armoury. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then, according to the statement, on this page where your initials appear at the bottom, you said: "Those were TO weapons which really belonged to the JNA." Now, I know it's your contention now that that's not the case, but that's what was written in your first statement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No chance I ever said this. That's how it reads, but I believe this must be a mistranslation. I simply couldn't have said this, because I knew who the weapons belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this, then, is a mistranslation. That's your explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said what you said about that in your language, it's your position that the translator translated that into English improperly and reported that you said: "These were TO weapons which really belonged to the JNA"? That's your position; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the investigator who was preparing this statement, of course, wrote down that mistranslation that he had heard from the translator, and so put in this English statement that you said: "These were TO weapons which really belonged to the JNA," right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then it's your position that when the translator read this back to you, the translator again, in reading the language which you had -- which had been written down as having been said by you, "these were TO weapons which really belonged to the JNA," mistranslated it the other direction, from English to your language and didn't read that to you correctly. That would have to be your position, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Maybe this simply didn't register with me at the time. Maybe I didn't hear that particular bit. I can't claim that it was a mistranslation, but my ears would have registered this had the person said this. I would have made the correction there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, where we started today, and you agreed with me that this was absolutely true -- where we started today was with you agreeing that you said on Tuesday that the changes required in the three statements were the consequence of problems in translation/interpretation and not errors of fact on your behalf. Now, you agreed with that. Do you want to change that now and say that wasn't the truth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing for me to change. This is how it happened. Now, how the mistake came about, whether there was the translation or myself not paying sufficient attention when the text was being read back to me in my language, I really can't tell you right now. But the statement has always been the same and will remain identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make sure and clear this in my mind. Witness, Mr. Sadikovic, could you go, please, to page 6 of your statement in B/C/S. Page 6, first paragraph, seven lines from the bottom of that paragraph. [B/C/S spoken] What does that mean to you? Does it translate into what has been -- you have been told by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just remind you of something Your Honour? This isn't what he said originally. This is the English being sent to the translation unit here. So it's not the original words either used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. I know. I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I just want to make sure that what we have in the B/C/S corresponds to what we have in the English. I know what you're saying, but I just want to make sure that what we have in the B/C/S is indeed what we have in the English version. Sometimes it doesn't tally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just thought I'd remind Your Honour of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you read there in the B/C/S version of your statement, is it correct or is it a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not correct. It simply can't be correct. TO is TO and JNA is JNA. Those were two different concepts, two different institutions. And I simply couldn't have said this, not a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to something different, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, what you told us was that instead of this being a translation error, that it might have resulted from you not paying sufficient attention when that page was being read to you in your own language. Is that what you told us? It's page 19, line 21 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I did say that. It's either a mistranslation or I wasn't paying sufficient attention when the translator was translating for me and I wasn't paying enough attention, perhaps. Because these interviews would usually take many hours. But this statement cannot stand as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when we talked a few moments ago about the oath that you took here when you started your testimony, you told me you saw that as being the same as the acknowledgment you made when you signed these statements. So if you were not paying attention when these were read back to you, in view of that acknowledgment that you made, were you also not paying attention when you were asked questions yesterday and today, and therefore not answering correctly because of that lack of attention? Can we make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't make that assumption, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in your testimony here in this Chamber, any errors would be errors of translation, not errors resulting from you not paying attention; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You went on to say then in your first statement, with regard to these weapons being taken by the JNA: "Had I been present, I would have not allowed the weapons to be taken." And my question is: How would you have stopped what appears to be several armed JNA soldiers by yourself? How would you have done that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wouldn't have done it alone. I would have woken the president of the municipality. I wouldn't have allowed the lorry to leave before a meeting took place in the morning, and someone took a decision, the relevant people from my municipality taking a decision whether the weapons would stay or go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you do believe that there was an ability there to prevent these JNA soldiers from doing what it was they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your -- in this statement, you of course told us that these weapons were taken from the police station. When you gave your second statement, and it's on page 2, paragraph 6. It's actually the first actual page of the statement, paragraph 6, you announced that that had to be corrected, that what you said in your initial statement that the weapons were located in the Kotor Varos police station was not correct and what you should have -- what it should reflect is that they were located in the Kotor Varos Territorial Defence armoury; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct, Your Honours. It's in the same building, one building, two different services. They have their own storage facility and we have our own. That is, we used to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then finally I want to, with regard to this issue, in your third statement, on paragraph 4 -- page 4 -- we've covered that, so I won't go into that. I want to talk with you now about the meetings that you had with Stojan Zupljanin. It's page 6 of the -- your first statement, your original statement, where you talk about meeting with Zupljanin, and what you say is that on 18 or 19 May, you were invited to meet with him at the CSB office in Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you tell us in that first statement that when you arrived in his office, that there was whiskey on the table.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was as we were sitting there, then Mr. Zupljanin's secretary brought the drinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the language that I'm referring to is in your first statement, sir. It says: "When I entered his office, there was whiskey on the table." That's the language I see in that paragraph that begins: "On 18 or 19 May, 1992 ..." And I think you have it in front of you and can see it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another translation error, or is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you now: I can't remember whether I said that it had been on the table or had been brought later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You wouldn't have said there was whiskey on the table if that hadn't been true, would you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason. I think it was, but this is a detail, and one can't really retain all the details in one's memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you don't remember that now. You don't remember when you arrived there that there was whiskey on the table, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I cannot say 100 per cent that it was there, but I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you recall it today, if you have a memory today of that, would you tell us whether it was in glasses or in a whiskey bottle or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we move, Mr. Ackerman, to the next question? Don't answer that question. Let's move to something different, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then went on to say that in addition to this whiskey being on the table when you arrived, that during your stay there, Mr. Zupljanin's secretary, Mira, brought in more drinks; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said this was a meeting that went on for three or four hours, and I'm just wondering if you drank quite a bit of alcohol during that meeting. And if he did too.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. It was all within limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what you've told us, and certainly what you said in this first statement, was that basically Mr. Zupljanin wanted you to deal with the people in Kotor Varos and get them to surrender their weapons, the Muslim people. Actually, what you say is this -- I want to be accurate: "He wanted to use me as a Muslim to deal with the people in Kotor Varos in order to get them to surrender their weapons." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said you were looking for a way out, so you asked him to give you a month or two to make a decision and establish your contacts in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I needed more time to talk people into something like that. I had to talk to very many people, go to every village, to every hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told him, according to this statement, this: "Come and put your flags up. We Muslims will leave our office with dignity and walk out." That's what I see in your statement. Do you see the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Zupljanin told you he couldn't give you a month or two, that he would give you seven days; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the next paragraph, sir, from the one we've been referring to, the statement says this. It says that you said this: "One week later, about 25/26 May 1992, I went back to Zupljanin in Banja Luka and told him that I would not accept his offer. He was not pleased and said he thought I was smarter than this. The meeting this time only lasted for about five minutes. Zupljanin stated that they, meaning the Serbs, would follow their plans and go into Kotor Varos." Now, that's what appears in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then when you returned from this meeting, you reported to Anto Mandic, you say, what it was that had happened. Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just remind the Chamber who Anto Mandic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Anto Mandic was the president of the assembly of the municipality of Kotor Varos and the president of the HDZ in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at your second statement, sir, this is the one of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 12 October 2000, on the first page, paragraph 8, you say that what your first statement reports about: "We Muslims will leave our office with dignity and walk out" was incorrect, that what you actually said was: "We Muslims will leave our offices peacefully and with dignity and walk out, but don't hurt the people." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's your position that this is another double translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely added something. It was not an error. I merely added the word "with dignity." And now, I can't find it. When I find it, I'll give you exactly the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me what you're looking for. Maybe I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second statement, the one of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 2, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It starts with [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Are you talking about the 10th of March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking of the statement of the 12th of October of the year 2000, the second statement. The first page, bottom half of the first page, there is a paragraph numbered 8, starting with [B/C/S spoken]. This is what Mr. Ackerman referred you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Which page, edition 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Page 1, at the top right-hand corner, you see a printed number, Prijevod 03007069. Then down to the second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine, Your Honours. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman wants to know whether this is another case of mistaken or erroneous translation, and I -- if I read you well when you started answering that question, you said: No, this wasn't a mistake. I just wanted to add, give more information, clarify my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I merely added. It wasn't an error. It was only -- but leave the people alone. Don't hurt the people. And we shall leave with dignity. And perhaps I said it even then. I can't recollect. But this is what was missing: "Don't hurt people" or "leave people alone." And that was the gist, the most important part of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you saying that you said that in your first statement and it wasn't properly recorded in your statement or are you saying that you added that when you made the second statement? It's important that you tell me which of those it is.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I realised that this was missing, because that is the heart of my sentence: Yes, we shall leave our offices, but just leave people alone. And that was missing in the first version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because you didn't say it the first time and then you added it the second time; is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours. And this is very important in that sense, in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told us this morning that all of the corrections that you had to make over the years were a consequence of problems in translation/interpretation, that was not totally true, was it; there were other reasons you made corrections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is natural. Perhaps there was a mistake on my part, because this was very important to mention. And if I didn't do it then, then I supplemented it, that is, added, in my second statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to your third statement now, and this is the one, sir, that's dated 10 March 2001. It's the -- I'm on page 4 of the English version. It's a paragraph that begins with the language: "In my signed statement given in 2000 ..." What you say at the end of that paragraph is this: "In my statement," that's referring to your first statement, "I'm quoted to have said that one week later, about 25/26 May 1992 I went back to Zupljanin in Banja Luka and told him that I would not accept his offer." Then you say this: "This is not correct. Zupljanin gave me one week to answer him, but I never did answer him, and did not meet Zupljanin a second time." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So my question, sir, is this: When your first statement reports at length that you went back to him on the 25/26 May and told him you would not accept his offer, that he was not pleased with that, told you were smarter than that, thought you were smarter than that, that the meeting lasted five minutes, that the Serbs would follow their plans, go to Kotor Varos, and that you went back to Kotor Varos and reported to Anto Mandic that you had had this meeting and what had happened, I take it it's your position that that whole bit of language there, virtually that whole paragraph, was a translation error, that you never said that you had a second meeting, but somehow it got into this statement. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I said that certain things could have been translation errors, but that naturally I do not remember every detail and every single thing. But as I think about things, as I roll the film back, then I -- then some things come back to me, those that happened, and in this particular case, it had to do with Mr. Zupljanin. But it is only natural, when one pulls his wits together and thinks, and then you realise that you went wrong there, and then I listened to what I said and I re-examined myself in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm now really confused, because I don't know what's true. I don't know whether you had a second meeting with Zupljanin or whether you didn't. So tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Your Honours. I didn't have a second meeting. Now, when I'm thinking about it, I didn't. I was to meet again with him in seven days' time, but I didn't, and that is why I made the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in 1997, when you made your statement, you just sort of made this up that you had had this second meeting and that after this second meeting you went and saw Anto Mandic and reported to him that you had had this second meeting and told him what had happened? You just made all that up in 1996 or 1997?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did not make it up. I reported to Mandic about the first meeting, what we had talked. But there was an understanding that I would go back in seven days' time. But I didn't. There was some reason why I didn't. But we were supposed to meet again in seven days' time. However, there was some objective reason for which I did not meet with him again and merely spoke to him on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you said in that first statement, you told the investigators that you had had this second meeting with Zupljanin. My question is: Where did that come from? Did you just make that up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no reason to make anything up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Did you just make it up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did not make it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then the only conclusion I think we can come to, sir, is that you told that to the investigators because you believed, four or five years after the event, that you had in fact actually had a second meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then why would I make corrections, after I had read it? Then why would have I corrected it? It would have stayed in the way I had worded it the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just asked the question that I've been trying to ask you. If you believed that you had had this meeting with Zupljanin in 1997 and reported that you believed it, how did it happen to get changed then in 2001, or 2000? And when did that change in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whenever I give a statement, I always analyse myself, and I try to put the orders in a proper sequence -- the events in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a proper sequence. Excuse me. And I try to think if I went wrong somewhere and if I presented the events in the chronological sequence as they happened. And then when I realise that mistake, when I rolled my film back and when I registered this mistake, then I saw that, as a matter of fact, it didn't happen, that it had been agreed that we would meet in seven days, but there were some objective reasons. We talked over the telephone with the chief several times, but that meeting did not take place. And that was why later on in my other statement I said that that meeting did not take place. That there was a telephone conversation, but for some objective reasons that existed then, the meeting didn't take place, and that is, Mr. Zupljanin, the head, was too busy to see me. So he postponed that meeting several -- two or three times, and that meeting did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in all of your three statements, you've never said that, that he was too busy to see you and postponed the meeting two or three times. That's brand new today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is new, but there had to be a reason why we did not meet after those seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that what you're saying is that only after you reflect and have a chance to look at and read your statements can you tell us if you have made errors or mistakes, and I understand that. So with regard to the testimony you gave yesterday and today, we should not put much stock in it until you've had a chance to look it over and tell us whether you've made more errors and mistakes again; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, after all, these events happened so many years ago, so it is natural that there are mistakes, because nobody is perfect, and nobody can keep it all one's head. 98 or perhaps 95 per cent are quite accurate. Now, 5 per cent could be more or less accurate. Of course there are things that I'm not sure about, but it's only natural. I mean, those -- the times were such, and all the events were such, and after all, it was so many years ago, and one -- you cannot absorb it all and remember absolutely everything 100 per cent of everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So among the things you've told us the last couple of days, there lurks 5 per cent which is not accurate, and so we're stuck with the proposition of trying to figure out which 5 per cent you told us the last two days is not accurate, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a comment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, your objection is sustained. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask him actually which facts arising from his testimony of yesterday he has some doubts upon, if there are any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are there any from your testimony yesterday that is in what you call that 5 per cent you're not sure about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I corrected the things that I had doubts about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, again, you still, I take it, agree that the acknowledgment that you swore to with regard to these statements, or that you signed with regard to the statements you made, you treat the same way as the acknowledgment you made to these Judges to tell the truth here; you see those as the same obligation to be truthful, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've put this question before, Mr. Ackerman. He's answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin tried very hard to block your appointment and keep you from taking your position as deputy commander, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, he told you that you would never -- that you would never be able to assume that position you had been appointed to; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it really turns out that he didn't have the power or authority to block your appointment, and you in fact were put in that position, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but the president of the municipality, I personally, and the political top leadership in Sarajevo, both Muslims and Croat, everybody had to intercede, and that struggle went on for several months, and that would include also the intervention of the European community, which at that time came to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and it was January of 1992 before you were actually permitted to take that position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that Zupljanin had his own candidate in mind for that position, a person named Sejdo Tatar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Sejdo Tatar is a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you told us yesterday, it's LiveNote page 16, beginning at line 13, as why Zupljanin wanted to appoint Tatar, you said: "The reason for it was that this gentleman, Sejdo Tatar, was married to a Serb, and he thought," I think referring to Zupljanin, "that he would be able to manipulate him and that he would do whatever he ordered him to do." That's what you told us yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and that is how it was. Tatar was there all the time. He stayed there with the Serbs and performed the duties as ordered by Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so was it at this three or four-hour meeting that you had with Zupljanin where he told you that he thought he would be able to manipulate Tatar and get him to do whatever he ordered him to do? Was that when Zupljanin told you that or did he tell you at some other time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say that to me at that meeting. I had already been appointed and was performing my duties. But knowing Sejdo, what kind of a man he is, because he's my neighbour and so on and so forth, that is what I thought of him and that is how it was. He was there all the time. He was the only Muslim who was there throughout -- in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you saying that Zupljanin --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I mean executives. I don't mean rank and file law officers. I mean bosses. I mean people who held executive positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you saying Zupljanin never did tell you what he thought he would be able to do with Sejdo Tatar? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that Sejdo was a good professional, that he knew the job, and as long as there was such a man in the police in Kotor Varos, I wouldn't be able to go there and get the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, if you read his statement, he never said that Zupljanin told him that he wanted Tatar because he was married to a Serb and that he would be sort of -- one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's reporting what Zupljanin thought. That's the only way he could know what Zupljanin thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What he thought. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. He's thinking what Zupljanin thought. That's what he's reporting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Let me read it out to you. First statement, second page, last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the testimony yesterday, page 16, line 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in his statement, I said he said that Zupljanin said that if he needed a Muslim to fill this position, he would prefer Tatar. "I believe the reason was that even though Tatar is a Muslim and was married to a Serb woman, he was more likely to be loyal to the Serb cause than I was." And then he continues to say what Zupljanin said. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that conflicts with what he stated on oath Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. yesterday, then put it to him again and ask for him to clarify which one of the two versions is the correct one; and if he has a reason why they're different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It clearly does, Your Honour, and I'll be happy to do that after we have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before we broke, sir, we were talking about this business of Zupljanin and Sejdo Tatar. Let me read to you the answer that you gave yesterday, and this is on page 16, line 13. It had to do with you being opposed by Zupljanin and Tepic. Ms. Korner said: "Why were they opposing you?" And your answer was this: "Mr. Zupljanin told me something like he had heard that I was not a bad man but that he had already a Muslim in the police." And I think you said: "Sejdo Tatar, who was a good policeman, highly competent one, and that as long as he was there, there was no way I could make my way into the police station, and the reason for it was that this gentleman, Sejdo Tatar, was married to a Serb." And this is the language I'm mostly interested in: "And he thought that he would be able to manipulate him and that he would do whatever he ordered him to." Now, when you say "he thought that he would be able to manipulate him," am I correct in my conclusion that you're referring to what Zupljanin thought about Sejdo Tatar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question should be phrased a little bit different, Mr. Ackerman. When you say he thought that he would be able to manipulate him, am I correct in my conclusion that you're referring to what you think what Zupljanin thought about Sejdo Tatar. Because I don't think that at any moment the witness said Zupljanin told him what he thought.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's my opinion. I am entitled to an opinion of my own, and I do have arguments to back it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what you told us there was your opinion as to what Zupljanin must have thought; you don't know really what he thought, do you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't know what it was that Zupljanin thought, but he said that as long as he had a man like Sejdo back at the police station, there was no chance for me to be there and do my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. All right. I'm going to another issue now. In your first statement, on page 5, in paragraph 6 in the English version - and I'd like to get through this rather quickly, because I don't think it's terribly important, but I'm interested in it - you're talking about -- I'm going to read you the entire paragraph: "I recall that four to five tanks had been stationed in a fenced compound at Maslovare, and sometime in April 1992. The official explanation for this action given by the brigade commander, Slobodan Zupljanin, was that the deployment of these troops was a training exercise. I believe that was how Slobodan Zupljanin was referred to in documents captured by the BH army in Skender Vakuf." Now, if we then look at your second statement, the one from 12 October of 2000, that first page, paragraph 5, the first thing you say right at the bottom before that list of numbers, you say: "I've reviewed my statement given to the ICTY and would like to make the following minor corrections concerning information that is incorrect." And one of those corrections was what you made there in paragraph 5, that instead of Skender Vakuf, it should say Jajce and Sipovo. My question is: Is that a translation error or is that that you changed your recollection of that issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this must have been a translation error, because we never entered Skender. The Serbs held it for the whole time. But we did enter Jajce and Sipovo. Therefore, this must have been a mistranslation. But it certainly wasn't my mistake. I simply couldn't have said this, because we never entered Skender. It was all the time in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that raises what I think is a really interesting question, because I don't know that there's any way to translate Skender Vakuf into English in a way that turns it into Jajce and Sipovo. There's no translation there. What you say in your language is Skender Vakuf, and what we say in English is Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Ackerman, that the previous witness we had referred to you as Mr. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Almost as obsessed as you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true, isn't it, that there's no translation. When you say Skender Vakuf, it's translated into English as Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no other way to translate that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that couldn't be a translation error. I mean, you couldn't have said Skender Vakuf and the translator have said Jajce and Sipovo. That's just not possible, is it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I couldn't have said Skender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I should have put it the other way around. It's not possible that you could have said Jajce and Sipovo and it have been reported by the translator as Skender Vakuf. I mean, that just makes no sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it short. It's obvious that someone made a mistake. It's either you or the interpreters, or who translated what you are saying. Who do you think it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I could not have possibly made this mistake because I know full well where Jajce is, where Sipovo is, and where Skender is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to another question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another separate issue now. On page 7 of your original statement, you're talking about that day of 11 June 1992, when the convoy arrived from Banja Luka. In your original statement, you said: "On 11 June 1992, approximately 4.00 to 4.30 a.m.," and we're talking about Bajram at this point, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're saying that: "Approximately at 4.00 to 4.30 a.m., I did not go to the mosque for worship due to the fact that I had had a few beers." And that's what you said in your first statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you said that instead you decided to go check on the Muslim security near the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I met Mr. Slobodan Zupljanin in the evening. We sat there and we had two or three beers each, and in my religion, once you've had a drink, even if it was just a glass of beer, you could not go and pray, in our way, at least. That was the reason, and that's why I didn't go to pray at the mosque. And due to the situation, I made the rounds of all the mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you said then in your second statement to correct what was in your first statement, in paragraph 9 on that first page, you said, instead of saying, "I had a few beers," that it should have said: "I had had a few beers the night before in Maslovare." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I could not have had a beer at 4.00 in the morning, obviously. It was the afternoon before in Maslovare, with Slobodan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, some of us have beers in our refrigerators, and we could have beers at 4.00 in the morning, and I suspect you could have too if you wanted to. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 46, line 18 of yesterday's testimony. Ms. Korner indicated Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. she wanted to ask you what happened the day of the takeover, and you answered this: "That day, that is, that morning, I was in front of the mosque in my neighbourhood, that is, in my street in Donji Varos. I didn't go for a prayer because I thought I'd visit all the mosques and I'd see some people, and so on." So yesterday your reason for not going for prayer was that you thought you'd go visit all the mosques and see some people, not that you'd had a few beers; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not only point that out yesterday. That was the primary reason I'd had a few beers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My point was: You didn't mention it yesterday in your testimony to this Trial Chamber, did you? You said that the reason you didn't go pray was that you wanted to go visit the other mosques, not that you had had a few beers.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I didn't say that yesterday, but this was the reason, and that's my final statement. That was the reason that I didn't go and pray.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this mosque that you were at when the convoy arrived is this one we just talked about that's near where you live, Donji Varos, I think, and there had been some kind of security stationed at that mosque, I think you said since Ramadan.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the evening prayer, there were guards posted in the villages and local communes also, and obviously for the evening prayer too. In the evening, when a major number of believers congregate to say the evening prayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, but you're talking about 4.30 in the morning on the 11 June, that there was security stationed near the mosque. That's not in the evening; that's early in the morning. Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a prayer usually attended by an even greater number of believers than the one in the evening. The guard obviously consisted of the reserve police officers. One of the commanders, one of the members of the reserve staff, Mujica Selimovic, was there, and the rest of the patrol. It was a mixed patrol. There was a Croat man too. I can't remember his name. It was a regular patrol, inspecting the guard posts. They would just stay for a brief while, talk to the people there, and then go about their own duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I'm not talking about a patrol. I'm talking about the Muslim security that was stationed at the mosques. There was Muslim security stationed at the mosques, wasn't there, since Ramadan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is an error, Your Honours. Guards around the mosque and down that street, along that street, but not in the mosques. There was never a single armed man inside the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me just -- let me read for you, and maybe it was -- let me just read the exact language: "On 11 June 1992, approximately 4.00 to 4.30 a.m., I did not go to the mosque for worship, due to the fact that I had had a few beers. Instead, I decided to go and check on the Muslim security we had stationed near the mosque since Ramadan." Now, is that an accurate statement? Was there Muslim security stationed near the mosque since Ramadan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never just Muslim guards. It was a mixed guard. And yes, there was security near the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is this a translation error in your first statement, where it says "Muslim security"? Is that another one of those translation errors that you've found?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. I'll leave it up to you to be the judge of that. I can only say that we always had mixed patrols and that our Croat neighbours themselves insisted to be included on that and to be part of the patrols and security. We had very, very good neighbourly relations, and that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't difficult for you to say on Tuesday, when you met with the Prosecutor and said all of these changes made over the years in your statements were the result of translation errors. And now today it's difficult for you to say whether this is a translation error or not. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we were speaking about one change, and that change was certainly related to a mistranslation, the change about Zupljanin and whether I came back several days later, that was my own uncertainty. I was not fully certain and I later made the correction. Therefore, I still stand by that statement. Now, whether it was my mistake originally or the translators, I don't think that's a substantial point really. Those who work simply make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your second statement, and I'm now on page 6 of that, and you're referring to this Muslim security.
