And here's what you say in your second statement: "Concerning my previous statement, page 7, paragraph 2, where I am talking about checking on the Muslim security we had stationed near the mosque since Ramadan, the reason that we had assigned security to this mosque is that we had assigned guards to all mosques because of the number of visitors during this period and because -- and not because of specific threats to the mosques." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it was for security reasons. This was discussed at public meetings in the municipality and at the station. This was not my personal decision. The decision was taken by the relevant offices in charge of the security situation in the municipality of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on that occasion when you made the second statement, you specifically directed your attention to the first statement, which talked about Muslim security, and you made no change in that. Today you decided that that ought to be Muslim and Croat security. That's the first time you've said that; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the first time. I've always claimed that, and I'll stick to that. It was always mixed. It was never purely Muslim. I may have failed to make a correction there. I'm not sure how that came about. But I state this under full responsibility. We always had mixed patrols, Your Honours, because that was what the patrols of the reserve forces were like, and then those guards too, throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there mixed patrols guarding the Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that. It was the period of Ramadan. It lasts for a month and then the period after that. But if Catholic believers were assembling in that week also in large numbers, of course we would have needed to provide security for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the security that you provided at these mosques during Ramadan and Bajram, that was to protect the mosques from what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the mosques; the believers assembled there in large numbers. So on their way out, to prevent incidents, there had been a number of provocations, drunken soldiers returning from the front carrying weapons and so on and so forth. The situation was tense in the town and in the whole of the municipality. It was just before the war. If you look at the dates, the war had already begun in Sarajevo and in certain other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go back to this day now on your first statement on 11 June of 1992, you then talked about this convoy appearing and passing where you were with this security force at the mosque, and you said this, and I'm going to quote exactly what you said: "As the convoy passed, some of those in our group which had weapons and rocket launchers wanted to fight. I convinced them not to do this, as I recognised this convoy was not like the other convoys of reservist Serb soldiers returning from the front." Now, then when you had an opportunity to meet with the Prosecutors a second time -- well, let me ask you a different question first. You said that you convinced them, that being this group that wanted to fight, you convinced them not to do this. And then you gave the reason why you convinced them not to do it. You say you convinced them not to do it because you recognised this convoy was not like the other convoys of reservist Serb soldiers returning from the front. Now, it's possible to conclude from that that if it had been a convoy of reservist Serb soldiers returning from the front, then it would have been okay for them to fight Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and attack that convoy; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your interpretation, which of course you're perfectly entitled to. I would not have allowed any kind of convoy to be attacked by young people, young and inexperienced people. I was a professional police officer. I knew how to sort such situations out. I would have acted under the laws then in force and under the authority that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that this -- that those in the group which had weapons and rocket launchers wanted to fight and that you convinced them not to do so. I take it if you had not been there, they may very well have fired on this convoy, because you had to convince them not to.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, you always get young and inexperienced people having their own ideas. There was talk of people arriving from Banja Luka to take over the power. Several dates had been set earlier, but it never took place; it never materialised. So some people realised that this was probably the convoy. So without thinking twice, maybe these people would have tried to stop the convoy from entering the town, and that's why I did not allow that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if in fact they had fired on the convoy, it certainly would have appeared to the persons in the convoy that they were being fired at from a mosque, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what -- no, fire wouldn't have been opened from the mosque. You couldn't do that. But from somewhere near the mosque. And what the people in the convoy might think, well, how can I know what they might think?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you revisited that issue in your next statement, what I call the second statement, and that would be the one of 12 October 2000, you changed what you had said in the first statement. You said this: "When the convoy passed our position, which was at the mosque at Donji Varos, there were no more than six to ten men guarding the mosque. We were armed with three automatic rifles between all of us, and one man had a Zolja with one shell, not a rocket launcher." So in the first statement there were rocket launchers; in the second statement there's no rocket launcher at all, but a Zolja with one shell. And then you say this: "To have fired on this convoy was not considered by us, because we were outnumbered and they had superior weapons." Now, when you said in your first statement that members of that group wanted to fight and you had to restrain them from doing so, was that a translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is no translation error. It is accurate, and you can check what this weapon is called. And whether I call it a Zolja or when you say a rocket launcher, that sounds rather superior, but this is something that any infantry man, any policeman can hold, and I merely wanted to call it its right name. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But when you said in your first statement that members of the group wanted to fight when they saw this convoy, they wanted to fight this convoy, and then in your second statement that you had to deter them from doing that, talk them out of it. In your second statement, you then say: "To have fired on this convoy was not considered by us." Now, those are two different things, and I'm wondering if your first statement there was a translation error or if you changed your story.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't even think about firing in any of the versions. I didn't change anything. I didn't correct anything. The substance is the same in either version. I was against opening fire, and I prevented it, and that is how it was, and that is the only way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So just to finish this: What you have just told them, told the Judges, the Honourable Judges, that the statement: "Some of those in our group which had weapons and rocket launchers wanted to fight. I convinced them not to do this" is the same thing as: "To have fired on this convoy was not considered by us," that there's no difference between those statements. That's what you want to tell these Judges?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there is no difference. I was against the shooting, and there are a number of reasons for it, except that I didn't list them all here. But I was, and I prevented it, and I stand by it, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you saw this convoy arrive, you told us that you went home, and with your automatic rifle and a backpack filled with warm clothes, jackets, medicine, and ammunition, you headed off towards the woods; that you left with a group of about ten men, crossed the river, heading toward Ravne. You then said in your first statement, on page 8, you said this: "When I got to Ravne, I first set up a kitchen and arranged for a group of our people to greet and assist the newcomers. I then established a headquarters in a small house, from where we first based our operations." If we go to your second statement, first page, paragraph 11, you corrected what you said in your first statement, from that small house being a place where you first based your operations to where we defended ourselves. So according to you, what your first statement should have said: "I then established a headquarters in a small house from where we defended ourselves." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: We were not either defending ourselves or attacking at that time, because it was early days only. So that it was the first day, and the second day. So it's the beginning, forming, setting up a kitchen, rooms where we'll be. There was no defence there. What I meant was the future time, the time to -- yet to come. But then there was no defence or attack or anything. These were merely preparatory organisation, discussing how to put up, how to organise ourselves, where to accommodate, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the fact is you changed your statement. You changed it from "where we first based our operations" to "where we defended ourselves." You specifically made that change. Let me suggest this to you: The reason you made that change was this: When you saw the language "where we first based our operations," that looked too much like you were engaged in offensive operations, so you changed that to look more like you were just defending yourselves. Now, that's what you did, and it had nothing to do with the reality of the situation, did it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Naturally, when I read operations, it sounded -- I mean, what operations? I mean, it's too big a word for the situation that existed there, because there were no operations later, let alone that first day. And that was why, because of this word "operations." That is why the change took place. So of course I wrote -- that is -- said -- because what I meant was our further action, that is, from where we defended ourselves and that is where our whole -- from where our whole organisation started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then your position that the language "where we first based our operations," it appears in your first statement, is another translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm repeating to you once again: It must have been an interpretation error, because of what I said. But late -- that is -- that's what they said. But later on when I read it, I realised that that was not the right word and that it simply did not correspond with the context to which that event was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As we've discussed before, then, it would have been a double translation error. It was translated incorrectly from your language to English and then translated incorrectly a second time when it was read back to you in your language. That has to be your position, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It is one thing when an interpreter reads something to me and I follow him, and it's another matter when I get that same text later on and when I read it word after word after word, when I think about it and analyse it. These are two different things. You know it just as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what's going on right here in this Chamber is I am asking you questions in English and an interpreter is translating those to you. So if what you just said is correct, your testimony here is likely to be filled with errors, isn't it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Let's move to the next, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's an appropriate question. I want to know if he believes that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not a question. It's a pure comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a speculation as well. When we had reasons to complain against the standard of interpretation, we did. But I think in the last year or so, we are -- I for one am full of praise for the standard of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So am I, Your Honour. I certainly wasn't suggesting that our translators in this courtroom were as bad as this witness believes the Prosecutor's translators were when they took statements from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this is getting -- this whole cross-examination is a question of Mr. Ackerman making speeches at the witness and I object to this. There are proper questions to put and there are not proper questions and what's going on at the moment are not proper questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you had left and gone across the river and over toward Ravne, somewhere in that trip you all kind of split up, and you went off to the village of Vranic, to what you said was to inform the people of the situation in Kotor Varos. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, while you were talking about that in your initial statement to the Prosecutor, you just mentioned that your wife and son had left Kotor Varos already at Easter to live with relatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. My wife and my son left on the last day of Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would have been what, March, April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did they have any difficulty leaving? Did they have to sign any of these documents you talked about or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It was still peacetime, and the situation was different. These documents came to -- to force following the 11th of June. Prior to the 11th of June, no documents were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to going to the village of Vranic, and what you did was you went there and told the people there that there wasn't going to be a Bajram this year, that they had to cancel the sporting tournament that they had scheduled, and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you asked them how many men were willing to join with you and the others in the woods to defend the non-Serb population from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask how many there were. I said to take care that everybody gets involved. There was a local commander, and that was his duty. I merely drew their attention to the gravity of the situation, to the hard times ahead, and so on. I didn't ask how many there were, nor did it matter, nor did I have any reason for asking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said in your first statement, and I'm at the bottom of page 7 and then going over to page 8, about this trip to Vranic: "I also told them what had happened in Kotor Varos and then asked how many men were willing to join with me and others in the woods to defend the non-Serb population from the Serbs," was that a translation error or did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it, because the number did not matter. I did not discuss the subject. It was later on that numbers came up, but then it didn't matter. I didn't discuss the strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Then you -- the statement reports that you said this: "I asked them to gather whatever weapons and ammunition they possessed and then join us at Ravne." Now, is that a translation error or did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not to join me, because they had to guard their villages. So I said weapons that you have. Because some of the weapons the citizens never produced, because they were either wise or because they were afraid to show it. They got these weapons out only after the war started, so I knew that there were such instances and I said that all the weapons should be put at the disposal and used, but they were not to come and report to me at Ravne. They were to be in their villages and stand guard there. I didn't need them at Ravne.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked about the possibility of finishing your testimony today and how it would be helpful if you answered my questions. So let me ask it again. Your statement reports that you said: "I asked them to gather whatever weapons and ammunition they possessed and then join us at Ravne." Did you say that or is that another translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say "to join us." Of course, to collect weapons, to get ready, but once again, I tell you I didn't say "to join us."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when the group gathered together -- that some of these -- I don't quite understand the sequence here, but there was a time when Serbs started talking to people over megaphones and suggesting they return to their homes. And you said that some of the people that had joined you actually did leave and returned to their homes and that after that happened, there were about 50 of you left, and that you considered to be the beginning of the resistance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, at Ravne, there were 50 [Realtime transcript read in error "15"] in Hadrovci, well, not literally in Hadrovci, there were for instance 30; in Doljani say 40; in Vranic 30; in Voljanci 50. But these were right next to me at the time and then the number grew and increased in other territories as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this 50 that you talk about remaining with you, I assume when it got down to that number, that everybody in that 50 had a weapon of some form.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. In the beginning, not everybody had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, nobody had a uniform, none of the people that were with you were wearing any kind of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were some hunting and suchlike, and some police -- belonging to the police reserve force, so that some of them were wearing those uniforms. But there were no proper uniforms or patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just to make sure that the record is clear, page 54, line 5, when I asked you about the 50 people at Ravne, you said at Ravne there were 50. The record says 15, but you said 50, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never say 50 exactly. I could have said around 50, 49 or something. It was never a definite figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with that. That's fine. In your original statement, your first statement, you talked about the people, this group of ten who went with you and crossed the river to go to Ravne. And among the people you said that were with you were the president of the SDA, Fikret Djikic, and a gentleman named Bakir Dizdar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No. Bakir Dizdar wasn't there. Later on I saw it was a mistake. I saw Bakir two or three days later. He couldn't have been with us, because he was in the centre of the town. That is where he lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I know you said that later. I'm asking you if in your original statement, did you say that -- and this is on page 7, near the bottom in the English, did you say that Fikret Djikic and Bakir Dizdar were part of this group of ten, that they were with you? My only question is: Did you say that in your first statement, or was that another error that you then corrected in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat it once again: Don't misunderstand me. I'm not saying that interpreters are not good and they are not doing their job properly. Perhaps I could have made that mistake. But I claim -- I put it to you that I didn't say that Bakir was there, because I know who those people who were with me were. I still know them, so that I really can say that I stand by what I said, that Bakir was not there that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you didn't say -- if you didn't say at your first statement that Bakir Dizdar was there, then I guess what you're saying is the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interpreter just sort of made up this name and coincidentally it happened to be someone who was in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought I'd make it clear. This really is not questioning. This is comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I was going to intervene myself. The position, Mr. Sadikovic, is this: That if you read the first statement, it does indeed say that you mentioned Bakir as being one of the persons that accompanied you. You also now are stating that you know that he wasn't one of the persons that accompanied you. What you're being asked is: How come that in the first statement you mentioned Bakir as forming part of the group? Did you make a mistake, which will not be the end of the world, or did someone else put in Bakir in that statement without you mentioning him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There is no way that I did mention him, because how else could somebody know his name [as interpreted]. So perhaps I did mention his name, but I also said that he joined us later. I'm not trying to dodge my responsibility. I'm not saying that I'm not making mistakes. After all, it is human to make mistakes. So I did mention Bakir, but not that he was -- not in that context, that he was with us that first day, but that he joined us later. Because I probably did mention him. Nobody else could have mentioned him except myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll try to explain to you what's happening here, because I don't think you are appreciating the exercise that -- or the reasons why -- behind the exercise that Mr. Ackerman has embarked upon. This all arises from what you told the intern from the Office of the Prosecutor that interviewed you last Tuesday. Because in that interview, you didn't say: I am making corrections because I may have made a mistake myself in one of my statements. You said that if you are going to make a correction, you're making a correction because this has become necessary, as a consequence of problems in translation and interpretation, and not because you were mistaken. And Mr. Ackerman is trying to prove you wrong. He's trying to explain that this was not the corrections that you made and that you continue making are not necessarily all of them tied up to mistakes in interpretation or errors in interpretation, but also mistakes that -- or corrections that have become necessary because you realise that you may have said something which was not correct or precise after all. So if that is the case, just say so. I mean, you're not under trial here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then there was -- we were clearly talking at cross-purposes. We can move paragraph by paragraph and I will tell you where perhaps I went wrong and where the interpreter went wrong, perhaps. But once again, and I underlined the interpreter did not commit all these errors. I mean, when I read it, I realised that things didn't fit, and that is when I made my corrections. But we go through this item by item and tell you where I changed it, when I realised that I had been wrong, and also say where the interpreters had gone wrong. And it is, of course, up to you to see whether that is how -- that that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clearer now. Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your first statement, on page 8, sir, and we're just moving forward in time. I mean, you've -- your resistance, I believe, has started now. And what you say then on -- in that first paragraph on page 8 is this: "We had control over all the high ground on the hills and were basically looking down on the Serbs in the municipality." True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that was our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You then talked about a skirmish, you called it the first skirmish and exchange of gunfire between the resistance and the Serbs. And I want again, just because it's important to be precise here, I think, I want to quote what you said in your first statement: "To the best of my recollection, the first skirmish and exchange of gunfire between the resistance and the Serbs occurred in the morning of 25 June 1992. The resistance was in Kukavice, and I learned that a few Serb soldiers were killed in this action." The reason for the action was that several young men from Kotor and Kukavice had gone back to their homes overnight and had been discovered by Serbs when they were departing in the morning to return back to Ravne. This action was not an attack organised by the resistance, but it just happened when they came into contact with each other." Now, that's what you said in your first statement. In your second statement, on page 7, talking about the nature of your position of leadership, what you said was this: "Their instructions," page 7, "were to conduct defensive operations only in their respective villages. There was never any plan to launch an offensive against the Serb forces. The plan was only to defend our homes and population." And then again talking about this situation in Kukavice on 25 June 1992, in your second statement, you said this: "Several of the men under my command were from the village of Kukavice. This night they went to check on their houses and families. When they were coming back the following morning, they came across a patrol of Serb soldiers. I was not present, so I don't know what actually happened, but there was a confrontation and some Serb soldiers were killed." Then we finally get to your third statement, on page 3, referring again to that matter. You say: "These soldiers were killed by a group of people from Kukavice. This happened on 25 June 1992. The group that was involved in the killing of Serbs was not under my command. I did not see the incident. I learned of it from one of the survivors from Kukavice." So in your second statement, they were under your command; in your third statement they were not under your command. Which was it? Were they under your command or weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that they were under my command. That's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when that third statement says that they were not under your command, did you say that or were you misquoted. Was it a translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how that came about, but what I meant to say was that this had not been planned. But I certainly couldn't have said that they were not under my command if they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So could it have been that what you meant to say was what they did, they did not by a command from you but on their own?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were under my command, but I was against them going to check on their houses and homes, for reasons of their own personal safety, and to keep their families out of trouble. I was against them going. But they went without informing me. I was against that, and they were under my command, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And so things were happening around Kotor Varos among these 300 to 400 men that were under your command that you really had no control over at times; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We're talking about a considerable number of people here. I can't always control all of them, because they are not staying put in one place, all of them, all the time. They're deployed along the lines of defence and they have their spare time, their free time. There's no way for me to monitor their movements or send people after them to monitor them. It's down to their consciences to decide where they would spend their spare time and what they would do in their own spare time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go -- I understand that. I want to go now to Vecici and what you said in your first statement about Vecici. You first said it was only one village in a large area controlled by the resistance, and that's a true statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours. Can I have the question again put more specifically, if possible, because I don't think I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your first statement, we're on page 9, you begin talking about Vecici, and you say: "The village of Vecici was only one village in a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. large area controlled by the resistance." My question is: Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you talk about how all Serb attention was focused on Vecici and perceived by the Serbs to be a resistance stronghold; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you tell that the Serbs actually shelled that village almost daily, from June through October of 1992, for almost a five-month period; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Not almost; every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were even attacks -- air attacks in June with napalm and cluster bombs on the village of Vecici; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in spite of all that, that village held out and did not surrender?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Am I supposed to answer? Yes, the village did not surrender, and it survived until the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these are people who you've described as being very lightly armed, with very little ammunition, holding out for five months against the vaunted professional army of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's correct. Resistance was put up, but in the meantime, they would arm themselves. Every Serb attack that they repelled, they would take some of these Serb weapons that had been taken, and day in and day out the number of weapons they had was increasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And finally, with regard to your first statement to the Prosecutor, I now have made it to the last paragraph. In the last paragraph, you tell us that: "Stojan Zupljanin, as head of the CSB in Banja Luka, is directly responsible for the actions conducted in Kotor Varos." Do you still maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I maintain that position. I do have arguments to back that position up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you just a second about -- I think you're going to agree with me this must be another translation error. In your first statement you didn't mention anything about a Crisis Staff in Kotor Varos. It came up first in your second statement, at page 4. That was the statement of 12 October of 2000. And on page 4 of that statement, you're reported to have said -- it's right at the bottom in the English version: "I'm not sure if Kotor Varos activated a Crisis Staff. They may have when the war in Croatia broke out." And then in your third statement, on page 2, you said that Kotor Varos definitely had a Crisis Staff, and no question in your mind about that. And my question is: Is that some kind of a mistake in your second statement, where you say you're not sure if Kotor Varos activated a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am certain that they did have a Crisis Staff. I just don't know in which period of time exactly it was activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that that's your position, but that wasn't my question. My question was: Is that some kind of an error when it appears in your second statement that you say you weren't sure that they had activated a Crisis Staff? Was that your error or was that a translation error?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say it was mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that just, you know, flip a coin and I'll pick one? Today I'll say it was my error?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday - and I'm at page 14, line 6 - you're asked about joining the SDA party, and the answer you gave was this: "Let me tell you: I joined them later, after I returned from the field in Croatia. And I think that in late 1991 or perhaps early 1992, they already had premises in the same place." My question is: What do you mean "the field in Croatia," "returned from the field in Croatia"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are people in the construction business, so every time we leave our municipality, we say that we go away on business, or we are in the field. My company, Kotor Varos, was a partner of Zagreb's Industrogradnja. We had construction underway in Istria, in Puja, in Medulin, in Rovinj, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was pretty sure that's what you meant. I just wanted to make sure. At page 18, line 16, you're responding to a question from Ms. Korner about communicating with the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, and your inability to communicate directly with Sarajevo because everything had to go through the CSB in Banja Luka. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that wasn't something unusual. That was the chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior for a very long time, wasn't it? That's the way it always had worked, or at least for a long period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's the procedure, and that's how our police station at Kotor Varos communicates with Sarajevo. We don't take the direct route. First it's us, then the CSB in Banja Luka, and then Sarajevo, and then feedback from Sarajevo, the republican station, and then it reaches the station in Kotor Varos. That's for as long as it worked. But at one point communication with Sarajevo was interrupted and instructions from Sarajevo were no longer valid and no longer applied to the chief of the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that had been the method of communication of every local police station in Bosnia-Herzegovina for a significant period of time, way before the war. Communications were from the local police station through the regional police, finally to the MUP in Sarajevo. That was the chain of command that was in place, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's correct. That was the chain of command under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You talked, on page 20 of your testimony yesterday, about television programmes, and at one point that you were no longer able to receive television broadcasts from Sarajevo. I take it that when you could no longer watch Sarajevo TV, that you could still watch TV from Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. I could watch certain programmes from Zagreb. They must have had very strong transmitters. So I could watch certain programmes, but it really very much depended on the specific area that you were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. On page 21 of your testimony, you were asked this question, line 1: "Did you, during the period between January and June of 1992, ever see Radoslav Brdjanin on television?" You said that you had, and then you were asked: "Can you remember specifically any of the things that he said on television?" And this is the answer you gave: "He said that Serb people needed it and that the Serb people had to do it and that the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina would be established and that it would be an integral part of Republika Srpska, and that all Serbs had to live in one state. That was the gist of it." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do. It was always pointed out how the Serb people were in jeopardy and that they had to stay in Yugoslavia, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that television appearance that you saw by Mr. Brdjanin, when he's speaking about the proposed establishment of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina had to have happened in 1991, since the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina was established in September of 1991. That makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I referred to a specific date. I'm not sure about this. But certainly it was proclaimed, it had been prepared and then it was activated whenever it needed to be activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I don't want to give you the impression that I'm suggesting that you talked about a specific date. You were talking about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a specific appearance of Mr. Brdjanin on television that you remember seeing, and what I'm saying to you is this: He said that the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina would be established. And what I get from that is he's talking about something that's going to happen in the future. And if it's the case that the Autonomous Region of Krajina was established in September of 1991, then this appearance had to have been before that. That's my point. And I think you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, of course. It had to be before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it may be that you didn't say everything you wanted to say about this, or that we misunderstood in some way. But at page 30, in line 17, Ms. Korner was asking you about patrols that were set up in Kotor Varos, and you gave some examples, and I think the second example you gave was this: First you said: "Every single evening, in the late hours of the evening, there was a van, a rather large van that could hold between 10 and 15 police officers or uniformed persons." And then you said: "Almost every night," rather than every single night, "the van made the rounds of certain locations in the town, and in the local communes of the Kotor Varos municipality. The van was carrying Serbs and the commander was Sasa Petrovic, who was always in that van, and they would make the rounds of certain points in town. And this was also very irritating for the citizens." I'm just wondering, if all that was going on was a bunch of Serb police officers riding around in a van, why did that irritate anybody?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It irritated people because mixed police patrols had been approved, and they were making the rounds, and that was enough. There was no need for any other units to be patrolling the town. Just on whose orders it was, it was very unclear. Of course it irritated people. We had mixed patrols, and our reserve forces were mixed in terms of their ethnic make-up: Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike were members of those patrols. And now it was the Bosniaks and Croats, then there would have been more people added to the guards. And if those were Serbs, then it would be Serbs. There was no need for further patrols. We already had patrols making the rounds that had been approved by the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to go now to page 38 of yesterday's testimony, and we start at line 5. You were asked if the Municipal Assembly had any authority to issue instructions to the police, and your answer was: "No. No. Under normal circumstances, that is, in peacetime, the interior affairs law, because we have one such, the Municipal Assembly could propose certain amendments or perhaps if problems arose, if things happened, then they could submit their own proposals, suggestions, and help us to overcome such problems in peacetime." If I understand that answer properly, you're saying that the Municipal Assembly had no authority to issue instructions to the police because of the law on interior affairs, that they could make suggestions, that they could make proposals, but they could not order. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the process of becoming a police officer, you told us that you had to take an exam and that you had to, I assume, study for that exam. And one of the things you had to become familiar with was the law on interior affairs; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: This exam did not entail the law on internal affairs, but it was for my own professional reasons, for my job, that I looked into it. I wanted to see what my authority was, what I was entitled to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fair. And in looking into the law on internal affairs, you learned that the chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior was from the local police, through the regional CSBs, to the MUP in Sarajevo at that time, and that the only civilian authority in that chain of command was at the very top, in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us where it is in that law on internal affairs that that situation is any different in wartime or emergency situations? Where in the law on interior affairs does it say that civilians can issue orders to the police in emergency or wartime situations? And I think the answer is that it doesn't say that; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding here. The law is clear and unambiguous. It only applies to normal situations, when there is no war. If there is a state of emergency, a different set of laws apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's enough, I think. Next question. Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a meeting in my chambers, and we need to be there at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you to stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will resume in 25 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm now going to page 40, line 3 of your testimony yesterday, and it's just an example of a question I want to ask you. In the process of answering the question you were asked, your answer, at line 3, begins with: "I can claim under full responsibility ..." And then just a little bit later, you say: "Once again, I say under full responsibility." And then: "I'm repeating under full responsibility." What is it you mean when you say "under full responsibility"? What does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special, Your Honours. It's a word which means -- one doesn't mean anything. I might have repeated it twice, but it has the same meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think maybe in your testimony you used it as many as 10 or 12 times, and I haven't counted them, so I don't know. But you seem to use that phrase when you want us to understand that you are absolutely telling the truth. Am I wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. Your Honours, when I am absolutely sure about something and what I know, then I emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to now look at a document. It's P150. This is a document signed by the infamous Milos, dated 20 May 1992. It says: "According to information which has been verified, during yesterday and last night," and that would have been the 19th of May, I take it, "Serbian citizens continued to move out of Vrbanjci, Kotor Varos municipality, and several other villages in this area. The majority of refugees have sought sanctuary around Celinac, Maslovare, and neighbouring villages with a Serbian population. At the same time, it was noted that citizens of other nationalities were moving out of these areas." And I want to stop there and ask you if you know anything at all about what's being reported there, anything at all about Serbian citizens leaving the area and going to Celinac and Maslovare and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I am a person who at that time held one of the executive offices in the municipality, so this had to be discussed by everybody in power. By all the authorities in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you understood the question. Mr. Ackerman read out to you from the report by a certain Milos, dated 20th May, which states that Serbian citizens continued to move out of Vrbanjci, Kotor Varos municipality, and several other villages in this area. What he wants to know is whether you know anything about what is reported by Milos and which was read out to you. In other words, whether you know anything at all about these Serbian citizens leaving the area and going to Celinac and Maslovare, at about the 19th of May, 1992. This is supposed to have happened on that day, during the day of the 19th and the night between the 19th and the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim under full responsibility that A, I do not know; and B, I'm rather sure that there were no such phenomena there at that time, at that time or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next part of that document says this: "A gathering of patriotically inclined citizens was noticed in the Maslovare area. They demanded weapons and to join military formations in order to oppose the extremists in the Vrbanjci and Kotor Varos area." Do you know anything about that happening around the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have with regard to that document. Thank you. In your testimony at page 44, yesterday, on line 22, you started talking about the availability of weapons in Kotor Varos, and you -- basically the difficulty of coming by a weapon in Kotor Varos during these early days of 1992. Your exact language, beginning at line 22, was: "It wasn't easy to come by a weapon. I have to tell you, in Kotor Varos, somebody else, you couldn't do it. Perhaps you could smuggle a rifle or two in your car, but to come by any major weapons, there was no way you could get into Kotor Varos bringing those," and so forth. Did you have any indication that persons might have been coming from other areas in the vicinity to actually buy weapons in Kotor Varos? Did you ever notice that or hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Weapons were bought in Banja Luka as a rule, because there was a significant concentration of weapons. And in Croatia, when the war stopped. And in the police, we were aware of this phenomenon, because it happened often that at a checkpoint, when a check would be carried out, that in a small truck or a car, one would find two or three rifles, and we knew about that because these things were happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I think your answer is that you don't have any information indicating people were coming from outside Kotor Varos to buy weapons there. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know about any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, at pages 68 and 69, you were asked about the killing of Lieutenant Colonel Stevilovic and others in an ambush, and you told us that this action was conducted by a person by the name of Stipo Maric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is correct. And others too. I don't know how many of them. But he wasn't alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Stipo Maric was a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Stipo Maric is a Catholic from Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And was he -- was he one of the members of your resistance group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you only learned about this two or three days after it had happened, I guess in a conversation you had with Stipo Maric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. He told me himself. They were coming back. There was a group of them, a group of men were -- and he -- in Vecici, and he was on his way back, and it was along that route that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the course of your testimony yesterday, you described him as a good man.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a very good man, but he was quite restless, could easily get into mischief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And some of the mischief he got into was ambushing Lieutenant Stevilovic and his group and killing them; right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's really not a question again. It's a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Ms. Korner's objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner's objection is sustained, Mr. Ackerman. I didn't stop you, but I was expecting Ms. Korner to stand up. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now at Exhibit P2001. You were shown this document yesterday and directed to paragraph 3, where the report talks about a sabotage attack on a minibus in the area of Kotor Varos, in which 13 of our soldiers, meaning Serb soldiers, were killed. And when you were asked about this yesterday, you said, and I'm going to quote your testimony: "Your Honours, I believe this refers to attacks carried out by a local group from --" and the transcript says "very muchic," but I think what you said was Vecici, "who can -- carried out reconnaissance and monitored the movements of those vehicles. They knew that another unit was taking over shift and they knew that they were soldiers on that minibus, not civilians. That's at least what I heard later. And that's when and where the action was carried out, in the Vrbanjci area. That's my opinion. I believe that's what it refers to." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Correct. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're saying that -- apparently you're saying that they were certain that when they ambushed this minibus, that it contained only soldiers and no civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is what I was told by people from Vecici, and that is what later on the media carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to look at P2448 -- 2248. I'm sorry. I said the wrong number. I apologise. This obviously is not the document I was interested in, Your Honours, so I think we can talk about it without looking at the document. You were shown a document yesterday that said something about negotiations going on regarding, I think it was a surrender and a transport of people out of the area, and you said that these were negotiations that you knew nothing about. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have to be concrete. Do you mean the negotiations organised by local group from the village of Hadrovci or do I mean the negotiations which took -- the official ones which took place in October with Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've found it. I've found it. It's the 71st meeting of the War Presidency on 3 September, and you've got it there. It's item number 2. "Tepic briefed the War Presidency on the contact made by representatives of the village of Hadrovci with the command of the company in Zagoni [phoen] who wanted to hand over weapons for guarantee of their safety." That's the issue I'm asking you about. And even though you were known as the commander of the resistance forces, you knew nothing about those negotiations, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I didn't know it. There were always people who acted beyond a doubt by the decision of a majority, and so this group too tried to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told the Trial Chamber about that on page 79, line 4, was, beginning at line 4 -- actually, line 5. "This is proof that I had no control over the whole territory." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You shouldn't take me literally. The whole territory. This was territory which we held too. Let's make that clear. But I couldn't control every individual man or smaller -- or every small group. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understood that's what you meant and that's the point I was trying to make. I want to talk to you now very briefly about Mr. Brdjanin. In your first statement that we've looked at a lot today, Mr. Brdjanin was not mentioned in that statement at all, was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the investigator didn't ask me about that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I understand that that may have been the case. My only question was he wasn't mentioned in that statement, and I think you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a fact, Mr. Ackerman. Let's move --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second statement, and this is the second statement that you were requested to come make by the Office of the Prosecutor. And I take it that that was the first time anyone ever asked you about Brdjanin from the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, during the first interview, nobody asked me that. Had anyone asked me that, then of course it would have figured in my statement. Of course I would have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking now about the second statement, and I think that was the first time you were asked about Brdjanin. I just want to point out what it was you said when asked about Brdjanin. You said: "I remember that one time on Banja Luka television in 1991," we talked about this earlier today, "in 1991 Radoslav Brdjanin said on TV that the Autonomous Region of Krajina should be formed and be separated from the rest of Bosnia and that new Serbian municipalities should be formed." Now, that's the same TV interview that you talked about in your testimony yesterday about seeing; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I watched it several times, but I can't remember various statements and conversations and so on. But I'm sure about that part in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then on 10 March 1991 [sic], you again appeared to make another statement, at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor. They wanted to talk to you some more?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 10 March 2001. And again, you were asked about Mr. Brdjanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this time, you remembered some more. You remembered that you had seen Mr. Brdjanin several times in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said that you heard him say that Serbs have to create the Bosnian Krajina for political and economic reasons. I assume that again is referring to that statement you saw in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you said you did not hear him make any derogatory comments against Muslims and Croats, although you had heard that from others. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I cannot say what I didn't hear. But I know concretely when he spoke about mixed marriages, how it will be resolved in Banja Luka, because Banja Luka is a town with a large number of mixed marriages, and so on and so forth. But I'd rather not comment on what I did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to look at the new document that you were shown this morning. It's P2329, please. Now, this document you talked about this morning, dated 27 October 1993, is a criminal report. It says that it's filed against -- and then lists a number of people. And item number 27 refers to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then it goes on to talk about civilians being killed during armed attacks between 24 July and 2 November of 1992. And I want to ask you to go to that section of the report. After number 29, it says: "There are reasonable grounds to suspect that during armed clashes between 24 July and 2 November --" and we understand that you left in October "as members of Muslim military formations, they look the lives of civilians." And it lists four people there, Tihomir Vasiljevic, Nedjeljko Popovic, Boro Lugic, and Nenad Novic. Do you know anything about the death of any of these four people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, and I do not think they are civilians. They are captured members of the Serb forces who had been taking part in the attacks. I am positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're positive that these four people, Vasiljevic, Popovic, Lugic, and Novic were captured by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the information I had when the attack took place, that these people were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then apparently killed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about them being killed. I'm not sure. But I know that they were transferred from that area into the village of Vecici alive, in order to reap the corn and stop -- and they asked the Serbs to stop shooting so that they could carry out the harvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you about -- there's now another person listed who it says was wounded, Dusan Pavlovic. Is he also one of those people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, Your Honours. I know neither the name nor the incident discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then finally there's a list of five people that said they were unlawfully deprived of their freedom and imprisoned in a prison in Vecici, where they were tortured and injured, with great suffering inflicted on them. And their names are Milovan Obradovic, Milenko Djuric, Drasko Sakane, Nedjeljko Djukic and Jelenko Tepic. Do you know what happened to any of those five people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know about that. I know that while they were in Vecici, once when I was in Vecici too, I talked to the man who was in charge of guarding those people and I told him expressly not to maltreat those prisoners, to treat them in a humane way and to wait until an exchange could be organised. Now, later, when they withdrew from Vecici, when they stayed behind us, as for that period, I really can't tell you anything about that, because I don't know what happened throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you would concede that they may have been mistreated in spite of your order; that could have happened, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, naturally. Real soldiers, proper soldiers, would never touch a prisoner. But you always had people like that who mistreated prisoners, who tried to mistreat everyone they could. There were always people like that around. That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to thank you for making an effort to answer my questions. Thank you for coming and sharing what you did with us. And I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, just one question, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, it was suggested to you by Mr. Ackerman, shortly before the last break, that -- he put to you: "Can you tell us where it is in that law on internal affairs that the situation is any different in wartime or emergency situations? Where in the law on interior affairs does it say that civilians can issue orders to the police in emergency or wartime situations? And I think the answer is that it doesn't say that; isn't that true?" I'd like you to have a look now at a copy of the law on internal affairs for the Republika Srpska published in the gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't copied this, because I wasn't expecting to have to do this but we will and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to Article 46?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can appreciate that. No one was expecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we get a copy on the ELMO or anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I've only got one -- oh, yes, we can. I'll put my copy on the ELMO and then we can read.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that say: "When executing duties relating to the protection of constitutional order, lives and personal security of citizens, protection of material assets from destruction, damage, or theft, maintenance of law and order, traffic safety, cases of general emergency caused by natural disasters, outbreaks of epidemic, the minister, an official authorised by the minister, or other authorised officials may, in cases of emergency, issue orders to citizens, companies, and other legal entities." Can I just ask, Mr. Sadikovic, is that what you were thinking of when you gave that reply?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's precisely the kind of situation that I was referring to, state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Sadikovic. That's all I ask in re-examination, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I make it an exhibit and I'll provide copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that would be Exhibit P2330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. P2330. Thank you. Mr. Sadikovic, we've got a few questions for you. Judge Janu is going to start. Judge Janu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, I would like to discuss with you two persons you mentioned in your testimony, and in your statements as well. First one is Slobodan Zupljanin, and second one is Anto Mandic. First question goes to Slobodan Zupljanin. I would like to take you back to that meeting which was discussed here by Mr. Ackerman, that he wanted you to stay on with the police force as a Muslim police officer. He wanted you to wear new insignia and to take new oath, and also he wanted you to get your people to surrender their weapons. And he gave you seven days for decision. And he also told you that you were to do as you were told if you wanted to be -- if you wanted to save your people. I think you will agree with me that he imposed great responsibility on you, telling you that you should obey or otherwise you put your people into the risk. In your testimony, you mentioned that Anto Mandic was president of the Kotor Varos municipality and also your friend. I suppose he was a Serb person, looking at his name, but I would like you to clarify this for me. And my question is -- and you said you discussed this meeting with Zupljanin with Anto Mandic. So my question is: What was the subject of the discussion? What did he advise you to do, if he gave you any advice? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he was the president of the municipality, so I informed him about that. It was my duty. But he was not the only person I informed about this. I informed my own president, Fikret Djikic. I informed him about the meeting and the discussion we had there. He couldn't give any answer or instructions. He just told me that he too had seen Stojan Zupljanin and talked to him, and that the subject of their talk was the same, the surrendering of weapons, staying in power, and so on and so forth. He didn't go into much detail, but it seemed that they had had more or less the same kind of conversation that we had had. Mr. Mandic is a Catholic. He's a Croat. He's not a Serb. By way of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question is: On what arguments do you build the responsibility of Mr. Zupljanin? Because you told us that you blame him for what happened in municipality of Kotor Varos. So I would like to know your arguments on which you build this conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one of the arguments, Your Honours. The special unit from Banja Luka could not be moved and could not go to Kotor Varos if this hadn't been ordered by Stojan Zupljanin. He was the main man of the police in the area. He had to bear the responsibility. Because all the orders were given by him, in cooperation with the Crisis Staff of the municipality. Every single order, every single attack carried out by the special unit in Kotor Varos and the other municipalities, none of that would have been possible without express orders by Mr. Zupljanin, orders in writing even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya, from Japan, would like to put some questions to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You testified that you entered employment with the Kotor Varos police force in September 1991. Concerning to this employment, you said in your statement number 1 that this employment was a political appointment. Does that mean that there was the commendation from SDA for your appointment? What does it mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to clarify this. The 1990 elections were held, legal elections. We know who won the elections. It was the SDA. The third place party in my own municipality, Kotor Varos. So after the regular election, when power was being handed over in order to balance out the ethnic make-up and structure, which was never properly balanced up to that point, the SDA, as the legal party of the Bosniak people, had the right to nominate candidates. I was not the sole candidate. There were at least three candidates from the Muslim ethnic group. But then that -- there is a further procedure. The SDA makes a nomination. This must go through the Executive Board of our municipality. Then the proposal is forwarded on to Sarajevo, and Sarajevo makes the final decision on appointments, whether it was myself or one of the other -- the remaining two candidates. That's what the procedure was like, and the procedure in this case was closely followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: According to you, what is the reason why you were chosen as a political appointee at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably my colleagues from the party knew me. They knew about my family background, about my education and my manners. They knew that I had had the experience of living in a big city, Sarajevo. That's where I studied. They knew that I was a person who had a wider -- a broad view of the world. They knew that I had not been involved previously with police work. But after all, I was not the only one with a more technical background to join the polices forces. But I think we did quite well, all in all, and I think we did our job rather well in the end. So that was probably the reason that my party mates decided to nominate me as the candidate. I was one of the three, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have just two or three questions. One is: You mentioned in the course of your testimony yesterday, and also somewhere in one of your statements, that, for example, there was an attack on Serdari and the attack was launched by a local group. I take it that this was a local group which was not under your command and over which you did not have any control. Were there any other such local groups operating in the municipality of Kotor Varos which did not form part of your resistance, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, some of those people were under my control, and some were not, and that was an HVO unit in Dobratici. They arrived in our free territory, and even back then we could tell there would be conflicts caused by the HDZ policies in Bosnia. And they arrived down there to take over command, and they wanted to turn us into the HVO rather than the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would not like to go into any further detail here. We did have our disagreements, but it was fine in the end. However, from that unit, there were a number of members of that unit who were taking part in that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the second of your statements, that is the one of 12th October of the year 2000, you state as follows: "It is my opinion that Stojan Zupljanin would not have conducted combat and police deployments to areas under his command without higher authority. I know that Stojan Zupljanin worked closely with the military commanders of the former JNA in the region, and there was a close link between the police, army, and politicians. All of these three structures were included in all levels of life and decision-making in the region." Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'll stick to that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say that you would not have conducted competent police deployments to the areas under his command, without higher authority, what or which higher authority did you have in mind when you made this statement? What were you referring or who were you referring to? Who would be a higher authority vis-a-vis Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been a misunderstanding there, a slight one, Your Honours. He had already done that, but he didn't do it of his own initiative, deliberately, or because he thought he was supposed to do it. It had been meticulously planned and predetermined how he was to do it, on which date, and in which neighbourhood. But he too had his own chain of command, control and command. It was no longer the minister in Sarajevo. He had his own minister in Pale, the parallel government that had been established throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, in Republika Srpska, that they had established. He had his own minister of internal affairs who provided his instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the chain of control and command that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say that he worked closely with military commanders of the former JNA in the region, could you indicate who or which military commanders of the former JNA he worked closely with? Any particular name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: It's only logical. It was the general from the corps in Banja Luka. That was his level. That's who he talked to and who he made plans with. More specifically, I have proof that when the MUP, Ministry of the Interior of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, when force was demonstrated at the Borac football stadium, we didn't -- or rather, the police knew exactly how many transporters we had, how many automatic rifles. They knew the specific numbers of the weapons that we had. It had all been provided by the JNA, the former JNA at that point. He had been given transporters, the BOVs, the combat armoured vehicles which had been painted from olive-drab into blue, and he obtained all the other weapons that he needed to be prepared for the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was the general? Can you name him? Of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I'm not sure if it was Talic in the early days, or I can't quite remember the general who was there. I'm not sure if I can remember both the first name and last name. I'm not sure if Talic was then the commander of the Banja Luka Corps or was it someone else. I'm not really sure. But I don't think it was Talic back then. Please don't press me on this, because I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for just one final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
